source.title: On the Limitations of Compute Thresholds as a Governance Strategy

record.file_problem: None; the full essay, appendices and references are present.
record.tranche_reason: The essay critiques the predictability of scaling-related performance and presents its own Open LLM Leaderboard comparisons, including large submissions scoring below the best small model. Its discussion of loss-scaling laws and fitting dependence otherwise relies on cited work rather than its own measurements.
record.gate_note: The leaderboard comparisons in Figure 3 are the essay's own analysis and are recorded below. Claims about pretraining-loss scaling, replication, irregular curves, and code-generation scaling are discussed through cited work and are not rows. Figure 5's cross-modality compute distributions do not measure power-law loss scaling.
record.test_reason: This is a governance essay. Its only original analysis is uncontrolled Open LLM Leaderboard comparisons across model families that differ in data, token count, post-training and compute. Parameter count alone is not the controlled scaling variable V6 names, and no loss, compute sweep or fitted law is measured. Its statements against V1, V2, V6 and V7 (replication issues, emergence, irregular curves, under 100 data points) all rest on cited work. So it discusses the claim rather than testing it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but misplaced in emphasis. The essay's main conclusion is that compute thresholds (10^25/10^26 FLOP) are shortsighted and likely to fail to mitigate risk. Its reasons are that the compute–performance relationship is uncertain and shifting (small models increasingly outperform large ones) and that we are poor at predicting downstream capabilities from scale. It recommends dynamic thresholds, a multi-metric risk index and better-specified FLOP.
record.recipe_differences: This is a governance essay, not a scaling-law reproduction. It synthesizes prior scaling-law literature and analyzes leaderboard submissions rather than fitting loss curves or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Leaderboard performance comparisons vary over time and across submitted models; model training and optimization are not controlled.

fits_no_version.finding: The best daily ≤13B Open LLM Leaderboard score rose from an average of 38.59% to 77.15% across about two years.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark performance at fixed parameter-count tier rises over time through data and optimization improvements, independent of parameter scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: A growing number of >13B leaderboard submissions score below the best daily <13B model. The text also names examples: Falcon 180B is outperformed by Llama-3 8B, and Aya 23 8B outperforms BLOOM 176B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across uncontrolled model families, parameter count is a poor predictor of benchmark rank.

record.problems: Leaderboard comparisons are observational and uncontrolled; model training, data and optimization differ, and the essay does not report uncertainty estimates or exact counts for the large models that underperform the best small model.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant results in the text meet the row criteria. Figure 5 describes compute distributions across modalities, not loss scaling; statements about power-law fitting, replication and downstream scaling cite other work.

untested.parts: No held-out loss measured against parameters, tokens or compute; only cited.
Architecture is discussed qualitatively only; no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Figure 5 shows training-compute distributions by modality, not loss scaling.
No controlled scale sweep or loss-to-downstream mapping. The argument against predictability cites Schaeffer et al., Ganguli et al., Srivastava et al. and Caballero et al.
Fit-dependence and replication problems are cited (Besiroglu et al., Caballero et al.), not measured.

record.verdict_notes: Changed relation from tests/T5 to discusses/T6. The only own-data analysis is the observational leaderboard comparison, which does not measure any version's construct. The essay's critiques of scaling laws are literature summaries, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The essay states that scaling laws have been shown for predicting pretraining test loss, but does not itself measure held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits or larger-run loss predictions are performed by this essay.
No compute-budget sweep or loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation is measured.
Architecture is discussed as affecting returns on compute, but the essay does not compare architectures at fixed parameter count and loss.
Modalities and training regimes are discussed, but no power-law loss relationship is tested across them.
The essay compares leaderboard performance across model-size groups, but does not measure performance against pretraining loss or conduct a controlled size sweep.
The essay reports literature claims about replication, irregular scaling curves and fit assumptions, but does not itself vary fitting choices or estimate exponents.

rows.subject: Best daily 13B or smaller model submitted to the Open LLM Leaderboard
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed leaderboard scores of the daily best small-model submission over time.

conditions.value: over the last two years; text also refers to 2024 submissions

rows.note: The essay describes the best daily small-model scores as rising from an average of 38.59% to an average of 77.15%; it does not specify the precise interval associated with each average. This is a change over time within a size group, not a controlled test of scaling.
rows.check: Time trend within one size group (best daily ≤13B score, 38.59% to 77.15%). It is not a scaling measurement. The baseline and value are averages over loosely defined periods, and 77.15% is the average across 2024 submissions. Link to none is correct.

rows.subject: Large models submitted to the Open LLM Leaderboard, compared with the best daily small model
rows.size_stated: Large models: more than 13 billion parameters; comparison group: less than 13 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared leaderboard scores of large submissions with the best daily small-model submission.

conditions.value: large models >13B versus best daily model <13B

rows.measure: Leaderboard score relative to the best daily <13B model
rows.baseline: Best daily model with less than 13B parameters
rows.value: The essay states that more and more large-model submissions score below the best small model; no score values or counts are stated.
rows.note: Aggregate trend over leaderboard submissions; the essay does not give the number of affected models or control for differences in data, training or optimization.
rows.check: The large (>13B) and small (<13B) submissions differ in training tokens, data, fine-tuning and compute. The comparison cannot show whether performance scales predictably within a controlled setup, which is what V6 names. No counts or scores are given. Unlink it from V6; 'reversed' overstates what an uncontrolled cross-family comparison shows.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Large leaderboard submissions (>13B) compared with the best daily small model (<13B)
reader_labels.reason: The essay reports that increasingly many large submissions score below the best small-model submission, contrary to a simple predictable improvement with scale (R2).
